 Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller
 The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.﻿
 The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.﻿
 by Andrew Liszewski 
 Andrew Liszewski
 Senior Reporter, News

 is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid. 
 Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it’s Jackery’s smallest power station to date, measuring only 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing just 1.87 pounds. Its size and 96Wh (30,000mAh) of battery capacity means you can squeeze it into your carry-on and power multiple devices during a long flight.
 The Jackery Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99. The power station is already available from Costco if you don’t want to wait, but only in a two-pack for $179.99. You can definitely find smaller and cheaper 30,000mAh portable chargers, but the LFP cells in the 100D are “engineered for up to 8 years of regular use,” according to Jackery, with a 3,000 charge cycle lifespan, so it should easily outlast competing products that use more common lithium-ion battery cells.
 Image: Jackery 
 Although the 100D is considerably smaller and lighter than Jackery’s other portable power stations , the company still includes an integrated handle and offers an optional shoulder strap for carrying it around. On the front, you’ll find a pair of 140W USB-C ports, plus an additional 18W USB-A port, but the 100D maxes out at 158W of total output, so power delivery across the ports will be reduced when all three are in use. If you need to charge it, can’t find an outlet, and managed to find room to also pack a solar panel, the 100D supports up to 100W of direct solar input, which will charge it back up to 80 percent capacity in about an hour and a half.

 EcoFlow has been a consistent top-performer in our tests, with one model earning the top spot in our guide to portable power stations. High-capacity, durable build, and reliable output are all strong with this line.
 So, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic with 45W solar panel for $479 (was $598) at Best Buy is an easy recommendation. If a power outage leaves you without heat controls, internet, or a working fridge, the Delta 3 Classic gives you a quiet, fume-free backup you can keep indoors.
 • Best for: Professionals, campers, and RV owners who want dependable backup power for outages or portable power on the go.
 • Why we like it: Beyond the strong performance in our tests, this EcoFlow model features 1,024Wh of long-life LFP battery capacity, 1,800W of continuous AC output to run big appliances, 3,000 charge cycles, and a five-year warranty. The solar panels for off-grid use sweeten this one considerably for us.
 • What you need to know: At $479 it’s good value for the battery alone, though the small panel is more of a bonus for added energy security rather than a serious charging option.
 Save $119
 Ecoflow Delta 3 Classic: was $598 now $479 at Best Buy A 1,024Wh portable power station with a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery rated for 3,000 cycles, 1,800W of continuous AC output with a 3,600W peak, and a weight of 26.7 pounds. This bundle includes a 45W solar panel and a protective bag, and it comes with a five-year warranty. EcoFlow sells and ships it through Best Buy’s marketplace.
 View Deal 
 Why We Recommend It
 EcoFlow is one of the biggest names in portable power, and the Delta 3 Classic is a pared-back version of its Delta 3 that keeps the essentials: a large, long-lasting LFP battery and enough output to run a full-size fridge or a space heater for a while. We haven’t tested this model ourselves, so this pick rests on EcoFlow’s track record and our experience testing other models. Expect fast charging, easy of use, and total dependability if you need additional or on-the-move power supply. The five-year warranty adds welcome peace of mind for a product you may rely on in an emergency.
 For more top picks, see our guide to the best portable power stations . 
 Price Context & Historical Value
 This is $119, or 20%, off the bundle’s $598 list price, which is a solid discount on a 1kWh power station with a five-year warranty. Keep in mind that the included 45W panel would take more than a full day of ideal sunlight to refill the battery, so think of it as a top-up tool rather than a full-blown charging solution. If you want backup power in place before winter, this is a good time to buy.
 Should you buy it?
 ✅ Buy the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you want reliable backup power for outages, you need enough output to run a fridge, router, or CPAP machine, or you value a long-life LFP battery with a five-year warranty.
 ❌ Skip the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you plan to rely on solar charging, since a 45W panel is far too small to refill this battery quickly, you need a power station that’s easy to carry long distances at 26.7 pounds, or you’d prefer to buy directly from Best Buy rather than a marketplace seller.

 Whether you are bracing for a storm-induced blackout or heading off-grid for a weekend of camping, a reliable portable power station is essential. The TechRadar team has put more than 50 power backups through their paces, testing heavy-duty home systems and compact travel chargers both in the lab and out in the field.
 The EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus takes our top spot for most users, blending generous capacity and rapid recharge times with a wide selection of ports. Plus, its near-instant 10ms UPS switchover keeps sensitive devices running seamlessly during sudden outages.
 We have also highlighted exceptional alternatives from Jackery, Bluetti, Anker, and DJI, with DJI serving up tailored power solutions for creators needing on-the-go drone and camera charging.
 Recent updates 
 What's new? We 've checked this list to make sure all the products still belong in this guide based on our reviews and availability. There's nothing new to update this list, but we did see the Vtoman FlashSpeed Pro 3600 has come to the UK, but as capable as it is, it's not good enough to justify a spot on this list. Do bear in mind we're entering a major sales period that'll peak wirth Black Friday and Cyber Monday in November, which means now is a good time to go on the hunt for a portable power station at a good price.

 Specs-wise, you’re looking at 1024Wh battery capacity, 2400W output, and a great port selection. For charging the device itself, you have the option of using AC, solar, car, or smart generator, making it a versatile device. .
 So, what was our experience using it? Well, we tested this device in the home office, garden, in a Jeep, and out on the road, and it proved to be a lot of fun. Operation was quiet, and we liked the rapid charging features and overall robust build quality. But what particularly impressed us is the UPS with a 10ms switchover, which means your core devices shouldn’t lose connection. During review, we simulated several power outages and our router, laptop, even lights stayed on for as long as the portable power station held charge.
 Price is admittedly high, and accessories are limited. However, for the cost, we found this unit delivered a solid balance of power, portability, and features, and an ideal solution for most uses.

If you need a lot of power for, say, your whole home or RV, this is one of the best out there. According to Anker, the unit will capably handle running an air conditioner, or even directly charge an electric vehicle. And after extensive testing, we can believe that.
 We ran a router, space heaters, and lights, charged laptops and iPads, and it handled everything we threw at it without issue. Port selection is excellent, boasting three UPS AC sockets and three standard AC sockets, a NEMA 14-50 AC port, L14-30R AC port, a DC port, three USB-C and two USB-A ports, home panel and dual solar panel ports, a car input port, and room for battery expansion.
 Beyond the sheer size, weight, and cost, the only real downside here is that we couldn’t charge up another portable power station using this device (and we tried - and the unit warned us of potential damage).
 Tip: Pair this with Anker's F800 Home Power System ( see our review ) for even more reliable home connections during blackouts.

 Reasons to avoid

 Jackery is a core player in the portable power supply game, and one of those brands you typically can’t go wrong choosing. For camping trips, though, I like what’s on offer with the Explorer 1000 V2, an update on the V1 unit that increases the power output and improves both port selection and overall portability.
 The capacity here is 1070Wh with a 1500W output and 3000W surge protection, capable of powering most household devices and appliances. In our own tests, we found it easily kept up charging three computers, a camera, drone, and lighting for the day. When we hooked up a MacBook Pro, it stayed fully charged with almost a continuous 100W power draw for six hours.
 We were delighted with the number of ports on offer - three AC sockets, one USB-A and two USB-C ports, and a car outlet - letting you power up a full suite of devices and appliances at once. Usefully, for those using this for work (or even at home), there’s also UPS, and when simulating an outage with a 3D printer, we experienced seamless switchover with no downtime when the power was cut.
 At 10kg, it might be slightly too heavy for some, and the 1500W output won’t power every household appliance, like irons, but if you're anything like me, you rarely take an iron on a camping trip anyway. For keeping your devices charged in the tent, it's ideal.

 Oh, and it's also a mini cooler.
 You read that right. The AC180T is part of Bluetti's SwapSolar series, which features changeable batteries and a multi-purpose cooler system and ice-maker all in one. When we reviewed this, we were delighted to find the system let us use the spacious Multi-Cooler anywhere while running on batteries - and when it begins running low, it was simple to pop it and swap it with another battery charging within the unit.
 It's aimed at campers, road-trippers, and travelers, and when we took this out on vacation to the cabin, we could see why. Performance proved to be fantastic as both a standard portable power station and as a cooler (it still feels odd even saying that, but there you go - the capability of this unit is great).
 Elsewhere, the power station is loaded with essential extras like UPS and a good but not extensive selection of ports.  The Pioneer Na is the world's first sodium-ion powered portable power station ('Na' being the chemical symbol for sodium in the periodic table). And that's gives it the edge over traditional lithium power stations, delivering superior thermal stability and reliability in cold weather.
 At 900Wh, battery capacity isn't ultra-high for the price (you're paying for the newer tech, really). However, in the team's tests, it easily handled powering a laptop, small refrigerator, and LED lighting all at once. Switching to the Power Lifting mode, it even powered high-draw appliances (in short bursts, at least).
 Design-wise, it's compact but relatively heavy at 35lb (16kg), and Bluetti has hardly innovated here. Beyond the light blue coloring, it stylistically fits in with the company's other offerings. What's especially good here are the tactile buttons, which are intuitively laid out and easily accessed even while wearing gloves.
 It also has broad appeal - we praised it as ideal for campers, RV users, and homeowners who want dependable backup in frosty conditions. Ultimately, nothing comes close to the Pioneer Na if you want a portable power station that works even in freezing temperatures.

 Tips for choosing the best portable power station for you

 Battery capacity 
Power station battery capacity is measured in Watt Hours (Wh) - or 1 watt of energy used per hour. The higher the number, the more battery capacity the unit has, the longer it lasts without requiring a recharge. To give you an idea of the power a unit has, an iPhone 17 Pro Max has a battery capacity of 20Wh; the cheapest and smallest portable power station in this guide has a capacity of 245Wh.
 Output 
Output measures the total continuous power supply a unit can deliver, and is measured in Watts (W). Small devices like a laptop and coolers tends to need around 60 to 100W of continuous power whereas appliances like fridges can need up to around 800W. So, a large portable power station with a higher output is best for powering large devices, or more devices at once.
 Input 
Portable power stations are usually charged via the mains - it's quick and efficient, especially for higher-capacity units. Many also let you charge the device from the car using a 12V cigarette lighter socket - ideal for those living the van life or in the RV. You can recharge some devices using solar panels, too.
 Solar 
Every portable power station I've selected for this guide have solar charging capabilities for off-grid power supply, but not every unit you can buy does. The solar panels can come bundled with the unit or bought separately. Smaller power stations will have a lower maximum solar input, making them slower to charge.
 UPS 
Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) is essential for ensuring reliable and continuous power even during black-outs. If you're using your unit for devices like routers or fridges, it's. Effectively, a UPS-enabled power station will step in during a power outage to continue charging or powering connected devices. Times vary, and while we're talking a matter of milliseconds, if it's a 'mission-critical' device, then select one with a faster switchover time.
 High surge wattage 
 This is especially important if you're using a portable power station on a job-site, as some tools, like circular saws, draw a huge amount of power at once. So, a unit with a high surge wattage (or high surge rating) prevents the machinery from tripping out the unit.
 Size & weight 
"Portable" isn't one size fits all. My team and I have reviewed everything from compact and handheld units to massive power stations that have built in wheels or need a trolley to move them. Depending on how and where you'll be using the unit, you'll want check the dimensions. As you'd expect, the higher the battery capacity, the heavier the power station will be.
 Ports 
Port selection is always worth checking. Portable power stations almost always include USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as mains outlets. However, larger units will usually have a higher number of ports as there's extra space for them, and the unit holds more power to charge more devices. Some go beyond this - for example, DJI's products include an SDC port for charging DJI drones on the go.
 Best portable power stations: FAQs 
 Are portable power stations worth it?
 Yes, but it depends on how often you use it and how many devices you're charging. There are a lot of models on the market, and the best portable power stations can handle everything from charging mobile devices and laptops to powering appliances and even EVs. If your needs are simple, you can pick up a good portable power station for around $200.
If you like going to campsites that have a power hookup they're not worth it as connecting to mains doesn't cost that much compared to a power station. For longer periods off-grid a generator is still, for me, the better option but for short weekend trips where you cannot get a power source these can completely change the weekend for the better if you want to keep using your tech or use electric-powered camping gadgets.
 What is the difference between a portable power station and a generator?
 Generally speaking, a portable power station is charged and outputs electricity. Generators tend to refer to units that use fuel like gasoline to generate energy and power. 
 Both can be used for back-up purposes, and both have different pros and cons. 
 Power stations are quieter, cleaner and more eco-friendly. However, their battery capacity can be low, and if it runs out of charge during a power-cut, you'd best hope it has built-in solar panels to re-charge. 
 Power generators are ideal for running heavy appliances, as they have a higher capacity, and isn't reliant on electricity, making it perfect for a back-up solution. 
 How many years do portable power stations last?
 A portable power station's lifespan depends on usage frequency and battery chemistry, but most last between 5 and 10 years with regular use. Like a phone or laptop battery, its capacity gradually degrades over time until it can no longer hold a full charge.
 THere are several key factors influence a portable power station's longevity: 
 The first is the battery type; models with Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries often last up to 10 years (3,000+ full charge cycles), while standard Lithium-ion (NMC) models usually last 3 to 5 years (500 to 1,000 cycles) before capacity drops to 80%. 
 The second and third factors, which we've combines, depends on a station's usage and storage; frequent deep discharges, exposure to extreme temperatures, and storing the unit fully empty accelerate battery degradation all affect its lifespan.
 How many Watt Hours do I need?
 Start by listing every device or appliance you want to power. For anything you'll run continuously — a fridge, a router, a lamp — multiply its wattage by the number of hours you need it running. For devices you'll charge and then use, like a phone or laptop, find the battery capacity in Wh (usually on the device label or manufacturer's website) and multiply that by the number of times you want to charge it.
 Add all those figures together and that's your minimum capacity requirement.
 It's worth adding a 20–30% buffer on top of that figure. Real-world capacity is affected by temperature, battery age, and the startup surge that motors and compressors draw when they first switch on.
 What can you run on a portable power station?
 So long as your portable power station has the right ports and enough capacity, it can run a massive range of devices, including phones, laptops, and desktops. 
 Higher capacity units will also let you power large home appliances and charge electric vehicles. 
 Check which ports your preferred model has, including USB Type-A and Type-C, AC and mains sockets.
 How long can you run a portable power station?
 It all depends on the power station and the device or devices you're charging. As a general rule of thumb, to figure out how long your portable power station can run, divide battery capacity (Wh) by power drawn by the device (W). 
 What is UPS and why do I need it?
 UPS stands for Uninterrupted Power Supply, and it’s a really important feature if you’re powering devices like routers and household appliances like fridges, or working on-site and need reliability. If you experience a power outage, the portable power station will automatically and seamlessly continue charge your devices without dropping the supply. 
 How we test the best portable power stations 
 Our team of expert reviewers have hand-tested a range of outdoor-ready equipment, including the best rugged smartphones , the best rugged laptops , and the best rugged tablets for working out in the field. We've even tested out the best rugged hard drives . So, we know what to look for when it comes to technology for rural locations and hostile environments.
 We test the best portable power stations on volume, weight, battery chemistry, and additional feature sets. Before writing any review, we try to fully understand the unit to describe each device's pros and cons best and accurately compare them. Part of this process is through benchmark tests, part is through daily use, and part is through simulated or real scenarios.
 As the main function of these devices is to be batteries, we test charge and discharge cycles on every unit. First and foremost, this is the most important feature of the portable power stations we test. If they cannot meet our standard here or do not come near what the other portable power stations in this guide are capable of, we will most likely not include them.
 Next, we push the power stations to their limits and beyond. We intentionally exceed the maximum power allowed on each generator, then observe and note the recovery from the over-power protection. This helps us promote safe power stations for you and your family.
 To ensure reliability, these tests are designed to learn the features, the downfalls, and the limits of the power stations tested by our subject matter experts.

DJI Power 1000 Mini: Final Verdict
 DJI ’s push into portable power has been surprisingly assured, and the DJI Power 1000 Mini Portable Power Station feels like the most deliberate product in the range so far. It takes the core idea behind the larger units and trims it down into something you might actually want to carry.
 This is a 1kWh-class power station that doesn’t feel like luggage. For creators, vanlifers and anyone working on the move, that shift in usability matters more than raw output figures, and might make it the best portable power station choice for them.

 The Power 1000 Mini is impressively compact for its class—closer in footprint to a large lunchbox than the typical brick-like power stations we’re used to.
 At 11.5kg, it’s not light, but it’s manageable in a way most 1kWh units simply aren’t.
 Compared to the DJI Power 2000 Portable Power Station, the difference is immediate.
 The 2000 is something you plan around; the Mini is something you just take.

 Small touches help. The integrated retractable USB-C cable is one of those features you don’t think about until you use it—then wonder why everyone else hasn’t done it.
 The front display is equally straightforward, showing charge level, estimated runtime and live input/output figures clearly at a glance.
 Outdoor visibility is generally good, although direct sunlight can wash it out slightly.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Performance 
 In use, the Power 1000 Mini delivers exactly what its size suggests. It’s ideal for:
 - Charging laptops, drones and camera gear
 - Running small appliances
 - Acting as a mobile workstation power hub
 The 800W output ceiling means it’s not built for high-draw appliances like kettles or heaters, and that’s the key limitation. But within its intended scope, it performs reliably.
 DJI’s use of LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) battery chemistry is also reassuring at this price point. Compared to older lithium-ion designs, LFP offers better thermal stability and significantly improved longevity, which helps justify the investment for anyone expecting to use the unit regularly over several years.
 Charging speed is a genuine highlight. Being able to push the battery up to 80% in around an hour makes it far more flexible than older, slower-charging units. Rather than relying on overnight charging, the Mini feels built for quick top-ups between shoots, journeys or campsite stops.
 Thermals are impressively well controlled too. Even during rapid charging, the unit never became noticeably hot in our testing, with only a small amount of warmth around the ventilation areas under sustained load. Noise levels are similarly restrained. Fan noise is minimal during general use and remains surprisingly subdued while charging—quiet enough that it largely disappears into the background in a home office or campervan environment.
 By comparison, the larger DJI Power 2000 does produce slightly more audible fan noise when charging, although the difference isn’t dramatic.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Front-facing light 
 One feature that’s easy to overlook until you actually need it is the integrated front light built into the Power 1000 Mini.
 Positioned across the front panel, it’s bright enough to be genuinely useful around a campsite, during a power cut, or when packing down camera gear late in the evening. DJI includes multiple brightness levels alongside an emergency flashing mode, turning the unit into something closer to a practical utility device than simply a battery box.
 It’s not powerful enough to replace a dedicated lantern or work light, but it’s far more functional than the token LEDs many rivals include. More importantly, it reinforces the portable, grab-and-go nature of the Power 1000 Mini—everything you need is integrated into the unit itself.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Accessories & real-world testing 
 DJI supplied a car charging solution for testing (the DJI Power Car Battery Charging Cable), but we weren’t able to fully evaluate it.
 Our only available vehicle during testing was a Tesla Model Y, which doesn’t support traditional alternator-based charging in the same way as a combustion vehicle.
 That’s worth bearing in mind—this accessory is far more relevant if you’re running a petrol or diesel setup. Ideal for the van, RV or Camper lifestyle.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Solar panel experience 
 We also spent time with DJI’s 200W foldable solar panel, manufactured by IBC, and this is where the wider ecosystem feels less polished.
 The panel itself is functional and reasonably well made, but compared to alternatives like the Jackery SolarSaga 200W Solar Panel , it’s noticeably less user-friendly in day-to-day use.
 It feels heavier and stiffer than expected, setup is more awkward due to the multiple MC4 connectors, and the popper-style support legs are fiddly compared to simpler kickstand designs. There’s also no solar alignment indicator, making it harder to optimize positioning quickly outdoors.
 More disappointing was real-world solar performance. Despite sharing the same 200W rating as the SolarSaga 200W, DJI’s panel consistently produced lower output in identical conditions.
 On a bright sunny day, the Jackery panel could comfortably exceed 200W, while the DJI panel struggled to consistently reach 150W using the same placement and timing.
 Individually these are minor complaints, but together they make the solar setup feel noticeably less polished than the power station itself.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: DJI Power 2000 - quick comparison 
 The DJI Power 2000 sits above the Mini in DJI’s lineup, and the difference is largely what you’d expect:
 Capacity: roughly double (around 2kWh)
 Output: significantly higher, suitable for appliances
 Weight & size: much larger and heavier
 Use case: home backup and high-load scenarios
 In practical terms:
 The Power 1000 Mini is about mobility and convenience 
 The Power 2000 is about sustained power and versatility 
 They’re not competing products—they’re aimed at different kinds of users.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Features & limitations 
 The Power 1000 Mini largely mirrors the wider DJI Power ecosystem, but there are some important differences between it and the larger DJI Power 2000 we tested recently.
 Most notably, the Mini does not support AC back-feeding functionality. Unlike the Power 2000, it can’t feed stored power back into a home circuit or act as part of a more integrated backup power setup.
 For most users, that won’t matter. The Mini feels designed primarily for creators, campers and mobile users rather than full home backup scenarios. If your workload revolves around cameras, laptops, drones and lighting, the balance of portability and capacity makes far more sense than carrying a significantly larger 2kWh unit.
 If, however, you’re looking for something capable of supporting household appliances or acting as part of a more permanent emergency power setup, the Power 2000 remains the more capable option.
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Pricing & configurations

 - US: ~$570–$600

 - UK: ~£833

 DJI Power 1000 Mini: Accessories

 - UK: ~£45
 - US: ~$55–$60
 DJI 200W Foldable Solar Panel (IBC)
 - UK: ~£339
 - US: ~$420–$450
 (Image credit: Future) DJI Power 1000 Mini: Final Verdict 
 The DJI Power 1000 Mini is a carefully judged product. It doesn’t try to outgun larger power stations—instead, it makes a strong case for why you might not want one in the first place.
 DJI has managed something surprisingly rare here: a 1kWh power station that feels designed to be carried regularly rather than reluctantly.
 If you need something you can actually carry, use regularly, and charge quickly, this is one of the most convincing options in its class.
 If you need raw output and all-day appliance support, you’ll still be better served by something like the Power 2000—but you’ll feel the difference every time you have to move it.

results.text:
Bluetti Sora 500 review: I tested this 500W solar panel 
 Skip to main content 
 We handpick every product we feature. We may be compensated or earn commission from the links on this page.
 Shopping 
 I tested Bluetti’s Sora 500, and it recharged my 2,000Wh power station in a day
 This 500-watt foldable panel delivered 463 watts in my test and recharged a 2,000Wh power station in a day, though setup takes patience.
 By Tony Carrick , Special to Hearst Oct 26, 2026 
 Bluetti’s Sora 500 unfolds into 12 panels arranged in two rows.
 Tony Carrick Portable solar panels are an essential sidekick to my portable power station on camping trips, helping me keep the lights on, the RV fridge running, and the water pump operating longer. But while they can add days to a dry camping trip, their small size and average efficiency often lack the muscle to charge larger  portable power stations . You can solve this with larger solar panels or by daisy-chaining a few sets together, but then portability becomes an issue. Multiple sets of solar  panels get bulky, and I don’t want a campsite that looks like a solar farm. 
 Bluetti’s Sora aims to change that with its new Sora 500 solar panels , which put out up to 500 watts in a surprisingly compact size. I spent several weeks testing these solar panels to see how quickly they could charge my Bluetti 2,000-watt-hour power station. With their compact size and efficient design, they quickly earned a permanent spot on my off-grid camping equipment list. 
 Bluetti BLUETTI Sora 500W Solar Panel 
 $799.00 at bluettipower.com 
 Portability
 If you’re taking solar panels on the road for off-grid camping, you'll want them as compact and easy to carry as possible, and the Sora 500s are. The Sora panels weigh 28.4 pounds and fold down into a 22.4-inch by 17.5-inch square that’s just 3.3 inches thick. This makes them heavier than comparable portable solar panels, including the Jackery SolarSaga 500X and Zoupe bifacial panels, but their square shape keeps them more compact and easier to carry than bulkier panels that weigh a few pounds less. They slide easily among other camping gear in a trunk or storage.   
 At 28.4 pounds, the Sora 500 packs small but still takes effort to carry.
 Tony Carrick Impressive efficiency equals ample power output
 Power output matters for whether a set of solar panels can really extend a power station's life, whether you’re off-grid RVing or trying to keep the fridge and lights on during a lengthy power outage. Portable solar panels can be tricky because they often get significantly less than their rated max wattage than bifacial glass solar panels. Many factors sap a solar panel’s efficiency, including wiring, high temperatures, angle, and cloudy skies. As a result, you typically get only 75% to 85% of a solar panel’s rated output. 
 During testing, I found Bluetti’s Sora solar panels performed well above average. On a clear, sunny day with temperatures in the mid-seventies, they generated 463 watts (93% efficiency) at midday. By repositioning the panels periodically for optimal sun exposure, I fully recharged my 2,000Wh portable power station on a day with scattered cloud cover. It’s impressive performance for such compact Sora panels. 
 The panel folds accordion-style and snaps together for storage.
 Tony Carrick Setup can be frustrating 
 Anyone who's used portable solar panels knows they can be frustrating to set up, especially if you don't have another set of hands to help. The  Sora panels are no exception. The panels consist of two rows of six solar panels stacked on top of each other. They use four supports that pull out from the back of the solar panels, plus additional supports that sit on top of the top-row supports. The design works, but folding out all four legs to support the panels was frustrating. I set up the panels in a few minutes, but a second set of hands would have made it much easier. 
 In my experience, soft portable solar panels tend to sag in places, which can hurt performance and give the panels a sloppy, low-tech look. That's not the case with the Sora 500 panels. Once I set them up, they sat straight with no noticeable sagging. 
 Connecting to the Bluetti AC200 I used to test the solar panels was easy, in part because both were from the same brand.I also connected them to an Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 portable power station I was testing, though I needed an adapter cable. 
 While setting up the Sora panels was a little tedious, taking them down was easy. The legs fold flat and snap securely to the panels. Once flat, the panels fold easily in an accordion style. I didn’t have to fold and refold to get it right. Once assembled, snap straps hold the panels together. I had the whole set folded up and on the move in under a minute on the first try. 
 Who is it for?
 Bluetti’s solar panels have many applications. They break down to a small size yet still produce a lot of power, making them a great option not only for keeping an RV powered while dry camping but also for emergency backup power if you live off the grid or in a place where outages are frequent and long. Pulling the panels out of the garage, setting them up, and connecting them to a power station takes minutes. Once up and running, they pull enough power to keep a 2,000 to 3,000Wh power station going for days, depending on the weather. Like most soft portable solar panels, the Sora 500s are made from rugged material. You can wedge them into other gear in the back of a truck or in a garage without worrying about damaging them. 
 It’s a heavy panel with a fussy setup, but for RVers and off-grid campers who need to recharge a large power station, the Sora 500’s compact fold and strong output make the tradeoff worthwhile.

results.title: How to build a seriously comfortable car camping setup
results.snippet: The article explains how to create a comfortable car-camping setup by prioritizing shelter, good sleep, easy meals, lighting, cooling, seating, and cleanup without overpacking. Because gear travels by car, campers can choose roomy tents, thick sleeping pads, full-size bedding, sturdy cookware, and larger comfort items, while still considering campsite dimensions and vehicle cargo space. It compares recommended products across categories, including family tents and compatible footprints; insulated or compact sleeping pads, sleeping bags, pillows, and blankets; two-burner stoves, cookware, grill
results.text:
How to build a comfortable car camping setup: Essential gear 
 Skip to main content 
 We handpick every product we feature. We may be compensated or earn commission from the links on this page.
 Shopping 
 How to build a seriously comfortable car camping setup
 From roomy tents to better bedding and an organized camp kitchen, here’s the gear that makes a weekend outdoors feel like a getaway.
 By Shannon Ullman , Special to Hearst Oct 28, 2026 
 The right tent, sleeping gear, camp kitchen and other comforts can turn a basic car camping trip into a more relaxing weekend outdoors.
 Billy Cadden Some camping is about bringing what you need to get through the night; other camping lets you actually settle in. With your car parked nearby, you don’t have to carry everything on your back or cram it into a tiny pack. You can bring a mattress thick enough to sleep on your side, a cooler with ingredients for a real breakfast, and a chair you’ll happily sit in for hours.
 That doesn’t mean bringing half your house into the woods. A comfortable car camping setup is about choosing the few things that make the biggest difference once you’re there: staying dry, sleeping well, eating easily, and having a place to relax at the end of the day.
 The trick is knowing what deserves that extra space in your car. Below, I’ll break down a comfortable setup, from shelter and sleep to cooking, lighting, cooling, seating, and cleanup, with product recommendations for each.
 Everything you need for the comfiest car camping setup 
 Shelter and weather protection
 Car camping doesn’t have to mean sleeping in your car. A tent gives you room to stretch out, change clothes, and keep your vehicle free for gear storage or a day trip. Since you won’t be carrying it far, you can choose a roomier tent with enough height to stand up in and space for thicker bedding. Look beyond the number of people on the label: think about where bags will go, how much room you’ll need to pitch it, and whether the rainfly will keep the entrance dry when the weather turns. Here are a few products we’d recommend:
 Six-person or family camping tents
 A roomy tent can make car camping feel much more comfortable, especially when you want space for thick sleeping pads , bags, and a place to change clothes standing up. These three serve different groups: the Snow Peak is best for a couple or small family, the Teton gives larger groups the most space for the money, and the KingCamp is built for a longer, more elaborate stay.
 Best overall: Snow Peak Alpha Breeze 
 Best budget tent: Teton Hacienda 8-Person Family Tent 
 Upgrade: KingCamp Khan Villa 4-Season Bell Tent 
 Best overall: Snow Peak Alpha Breeze 
 Snow Peak Alpha Breeze 
 $549.95 at snowpeak.com 
 The Snow Peak Alpha Breeze is a roomy three-season tent for two campers or a small family, with a three- to four-person capacity, doors on all four sides, a 6-foot-1-inch peak height, and a vestibule that converts into an awning. Its airflow, headroom, and sheltered entrance make it comfortable for car camping, though the 22-pound tent takes more effort to pitch than a basic dome and costs more than the larger Teton.
 Best budget tent: Teton Hacienda 8-Person Family Tent 
 TETON Hacienda 8-Person Family Tent 
 $399.99 at tetongear.com 
 The Teton Hacienda is a spacious, three-season tent with an eight-person capacity, nearly vertical walls, and an 82-inch peak height that leaves room for cots and gear. A swinging door, full-coverage rainfly, and interior storage add convenience at a budget-friendly price. At about 38 pounds with a roughly 10-foot-8-inch square footprint, it needs a large campsite close to the car, and smaller groups will have more room for bedding and luggage.
 Upgrade: KingCamp Khan Villa 4-Season Bell Tent 
 KingCamp KingCampKHAN VILLA4-Season 4-6Person BellTent 
 $999.99 at kingcampoutdoors.com 
 The KingCamp Khan Villa is a four-season tent for four to six campers, with two sleeping areas, a central living space, and a 94-inch peak height. Its pole-free middle makes furnishing and moving around easier, while polycotton fabric, mesh windows, and adaptable walls help manage ventilation. At nearly 59 pounds and with a roughly 15-by-10-foot footprint, it’s best for longer stays when you need plenty of vehicle and campsite space. Using its stove opening requires following the manufacturer’s installation and safety instructions.
 Tent footprints and weather protection 
 A footprint goes beneath your tent to help protect its floor from rocks, grit and repeated use. It’s a small addition that can be especially worthwhile when you’ve invested in a tent you plan to use for years. Fit matters more than the label on the package: the footprint should sit beneath the tent floor, not stick out where it could collect rain. These picks fit different tents; they are not interchangeable with the three family tents above.
 Best overall for a compatible MSR tent: MSR Universal Footprint 
 Affordable for Kelty Wireless 4 owners: Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint 
 Upgrade for Copper Spur UL3 owners: Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint 
 Best overall for a compatible MSR tent: MSR Universal Footprint 
 MSR MSR Universal Tent Footprint, 2 Person 
 $54.95 at amazon.com 
 The MSR Universal Footprint adds a lightweight, packable layer beneath compatible MSR tents to protect the floor from abrasion and keep it cleaner during pack-up. It comes in multiple sizes, so check MSR’s size chart for your exact tent model and confirm the selected variant in the listing before ordering. Despite its name, it doesn't fit every tent and shouldn't be assumed to fit the Snow Peak, Teton, or KingCamp models above.
 Affordable for Kelty Wireless 4 owners: Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint 
 Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint
 $39.95 at rei.com 
 The Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint protects the matching tent’s floor without the measuring or folding a generic tarp requires. Made from 68-denier polyester, it measures 92 by 82 inches, weighs 14 ounces, and includes color-coded corner connections and a carry bag. It’s an affordable, straightforward addition for Wireless 4 owners, though it needs separate drying and storage when damp and won’t fit the larger family tents above.
 Upgrade for Copper Spur UL3 owners: Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint 
 Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint

 The best laptop power banks are a must-buy when you're working away from a power socket. After all, even the best laptops for photo editing won't run on battery forever. And with governments telling us all to stock up on food and prepare for power outages, a power bank is a great way of ensuring you can keep vital devices going for a few days if the mains electricity fails to flow.
 But, the best iPhone power banks won't be powerful enough to do the job. Instead, you'll need a power bank with at least 18,000mAh capacity, as well as the right ports to connect to your specific laptop.
 As an added bonus, with a power bank this powerful, you'll be able to charge your cameras, tablets, phones,and other devices too. To find you the best model for your needs, we've put our experts to work. They've been testing and reviewing power banks, as well as using them within their own workflows, in order to compile this list of the absolute best.

With 1,024Wh of capacity and 2,200W continuous output (4,400W peak), it provides ample power for charging multiple drone batteries, cameras, and other essential gear on location. The two USB-C ports (140W each) allow for fast charging, while the SDC and SDC Lite ports support DJI’s proprietary adapters for even more efficient drone charging.
 Weighing 13kg, the Power 1000 is not the lightest option, but its sturdy build and rounded handles make it easy to carry. The clear display offers essential battery information, though it lacks smart features like an app or battery health monitoring. Additionally, there’s no built-in light or wireless charging, which could be a drawback for some users.
 Despite these limitations, the DJI Power 1000 excels at providing reliable, high-wattage power for drone operators and creatives working off-grid. Whether you're filming in remote locations or need a dependable backup power source, this station delivers efficient, high-speed charging for DJI drones and other kit.

The second is its ability to charge up to five devices at the same time, with a maximum output of 300W. That makes it particularly well-suited for camping trips, weekend hikes, or emergency power situations.

results.text:
77 Best Items For Your Emergency Kit 2026 | The Strategist 
 Every product is independently selected by (obsessive) editors. Things you buy through our links may earn us a commission. 
 77 items in this article 
 11 items on sale! 
 Photo-Illustration: The Strategist; Photos: Retailers 
 Compiling a stash of emergency-preparedness items used to be a task many of us kept on the back burner — something we knew was important and we’d get to eventually. But eventually, we now know, might be closer than anyone thought. And while we’re not suggesting you start digging out an underground bunker and filling it with instant noodles , in the past few years we’ve come to learn that having a few things on hand before you need them will only help you, even if it’s just mentally.
 Most preppers, like Oregon’s Afrovivalist , Sharon Ross, equate preparation with peace of mind. “Once a person is prepared during a disaster,” she says, “they don’t feel the sense of urgency to go shopping for supplies.” So if visions of empty store shelves still haunt you, have a nice, calm look at our well-organized, detailed list of emergency supplies to keep on hand. To assemble it, we consulted recommendations from the CDC ,  Red Cross , the Department of Homeland Security , and the NYC Emergency Management Department . But those agencies give you only general categories, and we wanted specifics. So we interviewed 22 survivalists, preppers , bushcrafters , homesteaders , and emergency professionals about their favorite things to always have on-hand — and their advice to make your bugout (or bugin) the best it can possibly be.
 Here are their suggestions, broken down into categories based on your level of survivalist instinct. There’s a lot to sift through here, but you can pick and mix products according to your needs. For many, a leaner survival kit makes more sense than a military-grade one. “Simplicity is key when prepping,” says Prepper Press founder Derrick James. Especially as, in a worst-case scenario, you might have to haul all of this gear a considerable distance. “It’s really important for people to know what their limitations are,” says emergency preparedness expert Aton Edwards, author of the book Preparedness Now! “Don’t prove how strong you are by dragging around a 40-pound bag . Rage lift in the gym, don’t rage lift your bag.” And in any potential urban or wilderness survival situation, advises Steve Lancia of North Camp Survival School in the Hudson Valley, there’s one piece of gear you should always keep around: “A cool head.”
 Updated on October 28, 2026 
 We’ve updated this list to make sure our top emergency picks are still available and correctly priced. 
 If you’re not quite ready to build your own bunker, check out our first-time homeowners’ guide to getting prepared , and if you’re just getting started, we’ve got a list of 10 essentials you should stock for any emergency . 
 The Basics 
 Backpack
 Most preppers keep two bags : a three-day bag and a two-week bag. While you needn’t get too hung up on that, it’s not a terrible idea to have something that you can easily grab that has everything you need in it in case you have to leave quickly. Bushcrafter Mark Christensen recommends a “quality rucksack, or even a five-gallon bucket , which keeps your emergency gear together.” Survivalist E.J. “Skullcrusher” Snyder (whom you might know from his many appearances on Naked and Afraid ) likes the “tough and roomy” bags by Gregory , but if you prefer something more tactical, he suggests something by Maxpedition . Jim Cobb , editor-in-chief of Prepper Survival Guide and Backwoods Survival Guide magazines, likes the RUSH24 bag from 5.11 Tactical, saying that it’s “robust without being ridiculously huge.” And Lisa Bedford, a.k.a. the Survival Mom , loves the Presidio Tactical Assault Backpack from Flying Circle, because it’s “a very good size for teens and most women.”
 Edwards suggests an alternative to traditional rucksacks: the humble folding shopping cart . “If you aren’t physically fit, then lugging around a fully stocked go-bag can be difficult,” he explains. “So a folding cart will let you move around from one shelter to another shelter.”

They’re so durable, in fact, that some are specially designed to be used as a self-defense weapon, Coyne says.  For most preppers, recommending a first-aid kit off the shelf would be like Julia Child telling you her favorite flavor of Pop-Tart. They like to put them together themselves so they can pack them with, as Hawke puts it, “some dressings for real trauma,” including tourniquets, Israeli Bandages , and, in R.C.’s case, zip-tie restraints, though he wouldn’t really say what those were for. That said, Coyne calls Adventure Medical Kits “the best first-aid kits on the market [and] definitely the closest commercially available to what I would customize for myself.” Survival Mom has a different preference, saying, “it would be hard to find better medical kits than those sold by Dr. Joe and Amy Alton at Doom & Bloom.” Their company offers a variety of kits that cover everything from labor to gunshot wounds.  Food
 Now hear us out: It might sound extreme, but at some point, you’ll probably wish you had some food. Our experts all approach the food question a little differently. Homesteader Lisa Sutton and the popular YouTuber, Prepper Potpourri (both Michiganers, both grandmothers), are big fans of canning and dehydrating . These processes take a little know-how, but are ultimately very practical and sustainable , especially if you grow your own food. They both like the All American Canner and the Excalibur Dehydrator . If you’re not ready to make your own food, our experts recommend stocking your pantry with, ideally, two-weeks’ worth of non-perishable foods like canned and dried goods, and peanut butter . “Think of very very simple meals, like oatmeal, [and] meals where you can open up a can of soup or chili and pour it over the rice and have more calories and more servings,” says Survival Mom, who goes into more detail about this in her book. And make sure you get stuff you actually like: “Don’t stock up on beans and rice if you don’t eat beans and rice,” Sutton says. Cobb’s in agreement: “Store what you eat and eat what you store. Don’t go out and buy cases of special ‘survival food’ if that’s not what you’re eating normally — a disaster or emergency is the last place you want to add stomach upset to the mix.”   
 If you want more variety and are thinking of supplementing your stock with freeze-dried food, Survival Mom, Prepper Potpourri, and David at Preppers Survive like Mountainhouse . Sutton recommends products from Thrive Life , “because they are real food, not prepackaged, high carb, high sodium emergency foods” like typical emergency foods tend to be. Hawke likes MRE’s (which aren’t technically freeze dried and which civilians can now buy), beef jerky , and meals from a company called Wise Foods, whose empty containers, he suggests, can be used as toilets. And don’t forget condiments, he says. R.C. recommends any junk food since it’s “full of sugar and preservatives and is good for survival,” if nothing else. Rogue suggests “morale-boosting foods” like macaroni and cheese, packaged cookies, raisins, dehydrated fruits, popcorn, and chocolate. And Edwards points us toward “high-protein stuff that’s not very heavy” like energy bars and trail mix. “Because when you’re in a crisis situation, you are going to burn more energy than you normally expend.”

Cobb agrees, saying that paracord is “the traditional cordage for preppers.”

 A Plan
 Everyone recommends you have a plan, preferably written out, and, if not rehearsed, at least talked about and memorized by everyone in your family. “Because in those moments when you’re frozen in indecision, and you panic, you’re starting to make really bad decisions,” says Survival Mom, who explains that “what you put into place beforehand is going to help you make the best decisions in those very intense moments.” “To implement the plan,” says Kellog, “survival supplies should be stored in accessible places that are known to members within the household,” And you should know how and when to use all the items you’ve gathered and test all your gear. And be sure to store important documents, photos and other items all in one place. Rogue suggests a fireproof and waterproof bag for this purpose. Edwards adds that when on the move, you’ll want to keep those passports and birth certificates close to your person, rather than in a separate bug-out bag.

 Personal Hygiene Products

The compact, budget-friendly Bluetti Elite 30 V2 offers 288 Wh in a 9.5-pound package. For longer household backup, the 3,840-Wh Anker SOLIX F3800 can run a refrigerator for about three days and supports 240-volt applian

 A portable generator is one of those things you don’t much appreciate until you need it, whether that’s during a blackout following a storm or when your devices die on a camping trip. Fortunately, with many great portable generators on the market today, all you need is a bit of planning (and a few dollars) to never be without power again, whether you’re at home in the dark or out in the field.
 The picks below are based on expert recommendations and our own testing (done at campsites, at our homes, and even during a multiday blackout). Generators can be powered a few different ways: with gasoline, by burning both gas and propane, or even with the sun when you use solar power for a battery inverter generator — a newer option that’s a great choice if you’re looking to run a generator indoors.
 “Gas-powered generators create exhaust fumes, limiting the use to the outdoors,” says Corey Dandy, a manager with the hardware chain Aubuchon Company . “Battery generators are completely safe indoors or even in-tent.”
 What we’re looking for 
 Total capacity 
 The first thing to consider when shopping for a generator is just how much power it can store — and put out when you need it. A generator’s capacity is given in watt hours, a measure of energy that determines how much power a device can deliver, for how long. Essentially, it’s the amount of work a generator can do — for example, a generator rated at 100 watt hours could power a 100-watt lightbulb for one hour. (That would be a very small, weak generator!) Watt hours are given as a measurement of total capacity — a 4,000-watt-hour generator can deliver that amount of work starting from a full tank of gas or a full charge in its batteries.
 To figure out how big a generator you actually need, add up the watt hours required to run all your essential devices in an outage (or for an outing). Most manufacturers don’t list a device’s watt-hour consumption, so you’ll have to do some math: Multiply each product’s wattage (you can often find this on the appliance itself or online) by the number of hours you expect it to run. Some critical appliances, like a refrigerator, would need to run 24 hours, but you might only run a CPAP machine for eight hours. Not great at math? Kevin Feak, an engineer with Fire Protection and Safety Services , likes the simple generator calculators on sites like Lowe’s .
 But before you buy a generator that produces at least that number, you have to factor in surge. This is the temporary spike in electricity that appliances — especially those with compressors like refrigerators and window air conditioners — draw when they first start up before settling into a lower running wattage. “Surge numbers are really important to factor in when you’re sizing a generator,” says Feak. If two appliances with high surge-wattage demands attempt to turn on at the same time, it could overpower a weaker generator. Feak went on to say to ensure you factor in the surge demands for critical devices like medical equipment, sump pumps, and well pumps.
 Number and type of outlets 
 Many of the battery-power stations out there these days have myriad different outlets, from AC outlets, which are the same as those in the wall of your home, to USB and USB-C ports, for devices ranging from computers to phones, to direct current (DC) ports, which are often used to recharge a battery generator via a vehicle or solar panel. (You may recognize DC ports if you’ve driven a car with a cigarette lighter.) If you need a portable generator to keep multiple large home appliances running during a blackout, or even to charge an electric vehicle in a pinch, you’ll want a generator with several 120/240-volt AC outlets; if you just want to keep phones and lanterns charged, a much smaller unit with a few USB ports and an AC outlet or two is fine.
 If you regularly experience seasonal power outages but don’t have the budget for a larger whole-home standby generator, some of the bigger units we looked at (Feak advises looking for models with 240-volt output) can dish out enough power to run a whole house — but this requires the installation of a device called a transfer switch near your home’s main electrical panel. You’ll need to hire an electrician to install the switch itself (professional installation typically starts at around $500). Once installed, the transfer switch allows you to redirect power from the grid to the generator for the specific circuits you’ve selected by manually switching it over at the panel. Installing a transfer switch can be a worthwhile investment.
 Weight 
 Just because a generator isn’t permanently fixed in place doesn’t mean it’s necessarily portable . For this review, we’ve considered units that can reasonably be moved from place to place thanks to their lightweight or built-in wheels and handles, because the mobility of the hardware is of paramount importance here.
 Keep in mind that batteries are heavy, and for a comparable amount of power output, gas-powered generators — even when filled with fuel — are often lighter than battery-powered portable power stations. This is worth keeping in mind if you plan to charge with solar panels: Most panels include cables that are only about ten feet long, so unless you buy an extension cable, you may need to move the unit closer to wherever the panels can get maximum sunlight exposure. With some power stations weighing well over 100 pounds, that can mean hauling them up or down stairs and wheeling or carrying them across the yard.
 Best portable solar-powered generator overall

 EcoFlow Portable Power Station DELTA 3 Plus - With 220W Solar Panel
 $1,189 now 23% off 
 $919
 Capacity : 1024 watt hours / Outlets : 6 AC, 2 USB-A, 2 USB-C, 3 DC / Weight : 27.6 pounds (power station only; 64 pounds with 4 panels)
 EcoFlow’s Delta series has been a popular option since its launch in the roughly 1,000-watt-hour category, a segment that has since expanded to include models that now quadruple that capacity. The Delta 3 Plus is a Goldilocks pick, with the best combination of capability and ease of use we found in our testing. It’s capable enough out of the box to run critical appliances, light enough for one person to carry, has a very fast recharge time, has a user-friendly app, and can charge from multiple solar panels for extended use during outages.
 The Delta 3 Plus has a surge capacity of 3,600 watts, meaning it has an easier time starting demanding appliances, and it can recharge fully from a standard wall outlet in under an hour. In practical terms, that means in an emergency, charging the Delta 3 Plus for an hour at a friend’s house or a café can provide enough power to keep a standard refrigerator humming for about ten hours. If you want even more capacity, like many midsize power stations we tested, the EcoFlow can use additional batteries (they don’t have their own screens or ports) that stack on top, extending your storage and run time without the cost of another full Delta 3 Plus.
 The Delta 3 Plus’s real advantage is solar capability. While many units in this size class can handle around 500 watts of solar input, the Delta 3 Plus can accept up to 1,000 watts through two 500-watt inputs, meaning you can utilize more panels. That kind of solar capacity means that for a little more money, you can get closer to the kind of extended run time you’d expect from a gas or propane generator, but without the fumes, engine noise, or maintenance. EcoFlow offers both permanent rooftop panels and portable folding panels designed to store in a garage or basement and deploy in a yard during an outage. The portable versions avoid the need for professional installation (and let you take the whole system with you on the road).
 The Delta 3 Plus uses a standard XT60i connector, so you are not locked into EcoFlow-branded solar panels (though manufacturers often discount when you buy panels at the same time as the power station). A single 220-watt panel can recharge the 3 Plus in about seven or eight hours, though the unit does support pass-through charging, so it can still power appliances while it is recharging. Fully outfitted with four of EcoFlow’s 220-watt panels wired together in series, the unit can recharge in three to four hours under partly cloudy conditions, or in as little as two hours under sunny skies. EcoFlow’s bifacial panels collect energy from both sides and they perform best over reflective surfaces like snow, sand, or light-colored concrete rather than grass (slipping a mirror over the surface, under the panels, can boost efficiency).
 Each 220-watt panel weighs about 16 pounds and folds into a compact two-by-two-foot package roughly two inches thick, though unfurled it stretches into a strip that is seven feet long. Setup is straightforward, with built-in stands that help angle the panels between 30 and 60 degrees and simple plug-and-play connectors that make daisy-chaining panels together painless. Using four panels at once might make it look like a small solar farm spread across the yard, but even unfolded, the panels are manageable enough to store out of they way against a garage wall when they aren’t in active use.
 There are a few negatives: The included solar cable is only about eight feet long, however, which may make it difficult to keep the power station indoors while the panels sit outside in full sun. EcoFlow sells additional extension cables , but that’s another added expense. The real downside is cost: Building out a fast-charging solar setup adds up quickly, with each portable panel costing roughly $300, meaning a fully loaded array can add well over $1,000 to the overall system price, so choose a kit for the best deal.
 Looking for an even better deal? EcoFlow tells us that our former top pick, the Delta 2 , should be available through this summer. It’s still a very capable unit and can save you a little money if you don’t need the extra outlets and flexibility of the Delta 3 Plus.

 For those who want more out-of-the-box power than the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus can deliver and don’t mind the added weight, the Anker Solix F3800 can run kitchen appliances for hours with little effort. It also includes 240-volt outlets for high-demand draws, like an electric dryer. At nearly 4,000 watt hours, the power the Solix produces is closer to midsize portable gas generators. The chunky, 133-pound Solix is about the size of a standard carry-on suitcase, though taller, with a similar telescoping handle that makes it easier to move around. Front casters help it glide smoothly across hard surfaces like patios, hardwood, and carpet, but carrying it up or down stairs is a two-person job. In terms of output, the F3800 has enough capacity to keep a typical refrigerator running for roughly three days. The 240 volt port means you can connect the Solix to a wired transfer switch, or even charge your electric vehicle in a pinch .
 Anker’s 400-watt solar panels feature four adjustable angles that let you fine-tune their position throughout the day, so you can optimize how they face the sun: keeping them more upright in the morning and late afternoon, and flatter around midday when the sun is highest. Like EcoFlow’s panels, they’re weatherproof, so occasional rain isn’t a concern and, in a backyard with good southern or western exposure and few overhead trees, you could keep these out overnight. Deployed, the panels are enormous — more than eight feet long and about 40 inches tall. Folded for storage, they shrink to roughly 40-by-27 inches and about two inches thick, weighing just over 35 pounds each. With four panels generating a combined 1,600 watts of solar input, the Anker recharged in about 10 hours under partly cloudy conditions, though it can take from 3 up to about 15 hours, based on how strong the sun is. The panels feel substantial and well built, though their weight makes them somewhat cumbersome to move around. Solar input tops out at 2,400 watts — you can pair the F3800 with up to six of Anker’s 400-watt solar panels through the XT-60 connection, but at $600 per panel, maximizing your recharge time would add more than $3,500 to the purchase price of the F3800.
 Pass-through charging allows you to run appliances while simultaneously recharging the unit through solar. Plugged into a standard wall outlet, the F3800 recharges in about three hours. With extra adapter cables, you can position the solar panels as far as 33 feet away from the power station, which means you can probably leave the unit inside while the panels are cooking outside. Like most of the modern power stations, the F3800 relays its charge status, both what’s left and how it is recharging, on a clear display and through an app that works through Wi-Fi or, when the internet is down, Bluetooth.
 Like the EcoFlow, the Anker can use expansion batteries, letting you scale up the system to nearly 54,000 watt hours — enough to power an entire home for a couple of days in an outage. In this setup, a (technically) portable battery-powered system is as powerful as a gas-powered standby generator, which can produce anywhere from 10 to over 50 watt hours. That said, if you have those kinds of needs, you might want to look at a more permanent setup, since a system like that based on the F3800 — though more environmentally friendly — would come at a considerable cost.

 A common complaint about traditional gas-powered generators is that fuel can go stale during long stretches between uses, making the engine harder to start in an emergency. Dual-fuel generators, which can run on either gasoline or the liquid propane in your gas grill’s tank, help sidestep that issue, and tri-fuel models like this Champion can also run on natural gas if you choose to have a plumber connect it permanently. “One benefit to doing a dual-fuel generator is that propane will store much longer than gasoline,” says Feak. “So it will not lose its combustibility, so you can have it sit in a shed for five years and it’ll be just as combustible as when you bought it.” The ability to run on propane may also help you avoid long lines at gas stations during major outages.
 The Champion’s power output varies depending on the fuel source. On gasoline, it produces 5,000 starting watts and 4,000 running watts, while propane delivers 4,500 starting watts and 3,600 running watts. This model includes several features that make owning a gas engine easier, including a switch-activated electric start powered by an included battery, which is a major advantage for anyone uncomfortable with pull-starting a generator. It’s also engineered for easier cold-weather starts, a critical feature since winter storms are a common cause of power outages. While it doesn’t offer smartphone connectivity, a built-in display shows useful information at a glance, including power output and run-time data to help track maintenance intervals.
 Gas generators are never quiet, but the Champion registers around 68 decibels from 23 feet away, roughly comparable to the sound of an electric toothbrush held at arm’s length. More important, it includes built-in carbon monoxide detection that can automatically shut the generator down if CO levels become dangerous. “A CO monitor that will automatically shut off the generator if it detects too high a concentration of carbon monoxide is a feature everyone should consider, considering how deadly CO can be and how people sometimes don’t think about the placement and have these units too close to a basement window or an open garage door,” says Feak. With a full five-gallon tank of gasoline, the 224cc engine can run for up to 14 hours at half load, while a standard 20-pound propane tank delivers about 10.5 hours at the same load.
